title: Caelza FAQ
content:
[Caelza FAQ]
Plain answers to the questions a new owner asks. Cael, the guide, reads these
(they are part of his corpus, `guide/corpus.jsonl`) and answers in his own
voice; the facts here must stay true, so `tests/test_cael_corpus.py` checks
the ports, paths and names against the rest of the repo.

title: Caelza FAQ › What is Caelza?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › What is Caelza?]
Caelza is an agent that lives on your own hardware. It is three layers: the
Runtime (the engine: the agent loop, model providers, channels, tools, the
dashboard), the Mind (long-term memory that forgets what stops mattering) and
the Body (the phone's sensors and device tools). It runs on a phone, a laptop
or a small server, and the dashboard is at http://127.0.0.1:42617 on that
device unless you moved it.

title: Caelza FAQ › Do I need an account or an API key?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › Do I need an account or an API key?]
No. Caelza works with no account and no API key: a free local model, DeepSeek
R1, runs on your device and is the agent's default brain. A provider key is
the other door: it gives the agent a bigger brain in the cloud. You can add
one later at any time.

title: Caelza FAQ › What is an API key?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › What is an API key?]
An API key is a password for a model provider such as Anthropic, OpenAI or
OpenRouter. It lets Caelza send the agent's requests to that provider under
your account. Caelza keeps the key encrypted on this device and only ever
sends it to that provider. A key is set with `caelza config set`, for example
`caelza config set providers.models.anthropic.default.api_key`, which prompts
for the value, and never typed into a chat.

title: Caelza FAQ › What is a provider, and what is an alias?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › What is a provider, and what is an alias?]
A provider is who runs the model: Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, MiniMax,
Ollama, llama.cpp, any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. An alias is one configured
entry under a provider, named `<provider>.<alias>`: `llamacpp.local` is the
local model on a phone, `ollama.local` the local model on a hub,
`anthropic.default` a key you added. An agent points at one alias with
`agents.<name>.model_provider`; the owner's agent is `agents.main`.

title: Caelza FAQ › How do I switch the agent to a cloud model?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › How do I switch the agent to a cloud model?]
Add the provider's key, then point the agent at it:

```sh
caelza config set providers.models.anthropic.default.api_key
caelza config set providers.models.anthropic.default.model claude-sonnet-4-5
caelza config set agents.main.model_provider anthropic.default
```

The dashboard's Quickstart does the same through its "Bring your own key"
door. Cael keeps running on the local model either way.

title: Caelza FAQ › Which local model do I get?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › Which local model do I get?]
The ladder is honest about size. A hub with 16 GB of RAM or more runs
`deepseek-r1:14b` on Ollama; 8 to 12 GB runs `8b`. A phone with 6 GB or more
runs `DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B` (Q4) on llama.cpp; a phone with 5 GB or
less runs the 1.5B, which is good for chat and explanations and not reliable
for long tool-using jobs. Cael always runs on the 1.5B. On a phone the model
server listens on 127.0.0.1:8080; the models live under `~/.caelza/models`
(the app keeps them under its own files directory).

title: Caelza FAQ › Who is Cael?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › Who is Cael?]
Cael is the guide inside Caelza: he explains screens, settings, errors and
approvals in plain language, offline, with no account. He runs on the local
model, has no tools and cannot change settings or act for you; he points at
the next step. The agent is yours; Cael is the manual that talks. His persona
lives in `~/.caelza/agents/cael/workspace/SOUL.md`.

title: Caelza FAQ › What does the Cael button in the top bar do?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › What does the Cael button in the top bar do?]
Cael's face sits in the top bar of every dashboard page. Tap it and a panel
says what the screen you are on is for and what the next step is, in his
words, with no model needed. Below that you can ask him anything about the
screen; the answer streams from the Cael agent on the local model, and his
look talks while he answers. Escape or the X closes the panel. If Cael is not
set up as an agent yet, the panel still explains the screen and points at the
setup.

title: Caelza FAQ › What are looks?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › What are looks?]
Every agent has a look: a small pixel character, one piece per layer
(backdrop, body, outfit, hair, hat, face, accessory) in the colours you choose
(skin, hair, outfit, accent, eyes). It blinks on its own and talks in the chat
while the agent answers; it stands beside the agent's messages, on its chat
tab, in the agents list and on Home. A new agent is dealt a look from its
name; Cael's is fixed (the constellation hoodie and galaxy eyes). A look is
saved on the Runtime under `~/.caelza/agents/<alias>/look.json`, so every
device shows the same character.

title: Caelza FAQ › How do I dress an agent?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › How do I dress an agent?]
Open Looks in the dashboard's menu (`/looks`) and tap the agent, or go
straight to `/looks/<alias>`. Pick a tab per layer, tap a piece, tap a colour
per slot (or choose any colour), watch the preview, then Save look. Undo puts
the saved look back; Back to the default drops the saved look. A dimmed piece
comes with a pack that is not in your wardrobe yet.

title: Caelza FAQ › What is the Shop, and what is a pack?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › What is the Shop, and what is a pack?]
The Shop (`/shop`) sells packs of pieces for the looks. Starter is always
yours; Cosmic (Cael's own pieces) is free and joins your wardrobe with one
tap; Arcade is the first priced pack and opens with an unlock code. The
wardrobe is the list of packs you added, kept on the Runtime at
`~/.caelza/looks/wardrobe.json`, so it is the same on the phone and the
desktop. Removing a pack from the wardrobe deletes nothing: add it back any
time, and a pack you unlocked once needs no code again.

title: Caelza FAQ › What is an unlock code?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › What is an unlock code?]
A code opens a priced pack. It looks like `ARCADE-7K3PQ2M9-` followed by a
long signature, it comes with your purchase, and you paste it into the box
under the pack in the Shop and tap Unlock. The Runtime checks the signature
itself, offline, against the shop's public key; nothing is sent anywhere. A
code that is mistyped or meant for another pack says so. Codes are cosmetic:
they open pieces for the looks and nothing else.

title: Caelza FAQ › How do I use my agent's look as a profile picture?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › How do I use my agent's look as a profile picture?]
On the agent's customizer (`/looks/<alias>`) tap Save as avatar: a 512 × 512
PNG named `<alias>-avatar.png` lands in your downloads, with Space behind a
look that has no backdrop. Telegram, Discord and the rest take it as is. From
the command line, `python3 scripts/looks.py avatar <alias> out.png` writes the
same file.

title: Caelza FAQ › What is an approval, and what happens if I deny it?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › What is an approval, and what happens if I deny it?]
An approval is the owner's safety gate. When the agent wants to do something
its risk profile does not auto-approve (uninstall an app, delete a file, send
money, anything hard to undo), it stops and asks. Approving runs the action;
denying stops it and tells the agent why. Either answer is fine. Before any
package is removed, the Body snapshots the package list so the removal can be
undone. Pending approvals show on the dashboard's Home page under "waiting on
you".

title: Caelza FAQ › What is a risk profile?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › What is a risk profile?]
A risk profile says which tools an agent may use and which actions need an
approval. The `phone` profile auto-approves reads (battery, notifications,
the package list) and asks before anything irreversible. Cael's profile,
`guide`, is read-only with every tool denied. Profiles live under
`[risk_profiles.<name>]` in `~/.caelza/config.toml`.

title: Caelza FAQ › What is Shizuku, and why does it keep asking?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › What is Shizuku, and why does it keep asking?]
Shizuku gives the Caelza app shell-level control of this phone without
root: the device tools (packages, settings, screen capture, input) run
through it. It has to be started again after every reboot unless the phone is
rooted: open Shizuku and tap Start. Without it, the sensors still work and
the device tools answer "needs Shizuku". On a Termux install the same role is
played by wireless debugging (ADB) on the phone itself, set up by
`python scripts/setup.py`.

title: Caelza FAQ › How do I pair the dashboard?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › How do I pair the dashboard?]
The first browser or app to open the dashboard must pair. The gateway prints a
pairing code in its log; `caelza gateway get-paircode` prints it again and
`caelza gateway get-paircode --new` makes a fresh one. Type it on the pairing
screen. The Caelza app on a phone pairs its own dashboard shell by itself, so
no code is typed there, and no other app on the phone can use its gateway.

title: Caelza FAQ › How do I pair another phone?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › How do I pair another phone?]
On the Bodies page of the dashboard (or with the agent's `device_pair` tool):
turn on Wireless debugging on the other phone, read its pairing code and
address, and enter them. The agent can then read that phone and, with
approvals, change it. A phone running its own Body can instead be joined over
the network with `caelza-body fleet join` (or the agent's `device_join`), with
its token kept in a file, never in the chat.

title: Caelza FAQ › What is the Body?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › What is the Body?]
The Body is the device layer: sensors (camera, microphone, location,
notifications, battery, clipboard, text-to-speech, torch) and device tools
(packages, settings, screen capture, input, logs) on this phone and on paired
phones. Every dangerous action needs a reason, is written to an audit log
(`~/.caelza-body/logs/device-actions.log`), and a package list is snapshotted
before anything is removed. The Body is served to the Runtime as an MCP server
on 127.0.0.1:42618 behind a token file.

title: Caelza FAQ › What is the Mind?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › What is the Mind?]
The Mind is Caelza's long-term memory, built on xanima: it remembers across
sessions, keeps what matters and forgets what stops mattering, and sleeps to
consolidate. Ask the agent what it remembers, or tell it to forget something.
The dashboard's Memory page shows the brains, what is waiting for review, and
lets you recall or forget by hand. `caelza memory stats` is the command-line
check. On a phone the app runs it; on a Linux hub `mind/install.sh` installs
it; on a Windows PC `mind/windows-install.ps1` does, and the Start menu's
Caelza starts it with the Runtime.

title: Caelza FAQ › What are procedures?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › What are procedures?]
Procedures are step-by-step playbooks the agent runs with a gate before the
step that changes the phone: debloat a carrier phone, remove malware, set up a
new phone, run diagnostics. Start one from the dashboard's Procedures page,
pick the phone, and approve or deny at the gate. The deterministic parts (the
debloat plan, the suspects list, the health check) are read-only tools you can
run on their own.

title: Caelza FAQ › How do I connect my apps (Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Notion, Slack)?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › How do I connect my apps (Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Notion, Slack)?]
Through Maton, a service that keeps the sign-in to each app so Caelza does not
have to. Make a free account at maton.ai, connect the apps you want there, and
copy your Maton API key from its settings. Then open the dashboard's Connect
page, paste the key into the "Your apps" card and press Connect: Cael adds
Maton's server to the Runtime, keeps the key encrypted, and grants it to your
main agent. (The shell way is `sh scripts/maton-connect.sh`, which asks for the
key at a masked prompt.) Caelza picks it up the next time it starts; then ask
something harmless first, such as what is on your calendar today. The key is
never shown again; anyone who holds it can reach every app you connected, so
treat it like a password. Reading is free; sending, posting, paying and
deleting always ask you first.

title: Caelza FAQ › How do I connect my smart home (Home Assistant)?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › How do I connect my smart home (Home Assistant)?]
asks you first, and locks, doors and alarms always ask. This is new and has not
been tried against a real Home Assistant yet, so tell us if the token is
refused.

title: Caelza FAQ › Can Caelza watch my 3D printer?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › Can Caelza watch my 3D printer?]
Yes, for printers running Moonraker (Klipper, Mainsail, Fluidd) or OctoPrint, as
long as the printer is on the same Wi-Fi as the device running Caelza. Bambu Lab
printers are not supported yet. Caelza can tell you the state, progress, time left
and temperatures, and fetch a camera snapshot. It can pause or cancel a print only
after you say yes; it never starts prints, sends G-code or hits the emergency stop.
To set it up, open the dashboard's Connect page: the "3D printer" card takes the
printer's address (that one address is allowed, not your whole network), which
software it runs, and for OctoPrint its API key (kept as a secret); Connect
writes the config and installs the printer skill for your main agent. (By hand:
`runtime/caelza.printer.example.toml` and the skill in the `skills` folder.)

title: Caelza FAQ › Can Caelza watch my 3D printer?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › Can Caelza watch my 3D printer?]
Every request asks you for approval, reads included. This is new and has not
been tried against a real printer yet.

title: Caelza FAQ › Where do settings live?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › Where do settings live?]
The Runtime's config is `~/.caelza/config.toml` (the app keeps it under its
own files directory). Change it with `caelza config set <path> <value>` so the
Runtime validates every value and encrypts secrets; the dashboard's Config
page does the same. The Body's own settings are in `~/.caelza-body/config.toml`.

title: Caelza FAQ › How is the Runtime updated?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › How is the Runtime updated?]
Through the guard: `caelza-body runtime update` finds the release, verifies
its checksum, probes the new binary (`caelza --version` must answer with the
release's version and the gateway must serve `/health`), keeps the previous
version as `last-good`, and rolls back on a crash loop. The Caelza app does
the same by itself. Nothing is trusted before it is probed.

title: Caelza FAQ › Where do I see what went wrong?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › Where do I see what went wrong?]
The dashboard's Logs page shows the Runtime's log; the Home page shows
whether the Runtime, the Mind and the Body are up. On a phone with the app,
the status strip under the dashboard says what each layer is doing and what it
needs (Shizuku, a permission, a model still downloading). `caelza daemon`
prints its log to the terminal on a Termux install.

title: Caelza FAQ › How do I install it?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › How do I install it?]
On a phone, the Caelza app: it installs the Runtime, runs the first setup with
Cael, and serves the Body itself. In Termux, one line installs the Runtime
(`runtime/termux-install.sh`) and one line installs the Body (`install.sh`);
`scripts/model-setup.sh` fetches the free model and creates Cael. On a laptop
or server, build the Runtime with `./runtime/build.sh`, run `caelza
quickstart`, then `caelza daemon`.

title: Caelza FAQ › Can I use Caelza on a Windows PC?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › Can I use Caelza on a Windows PC?]
Experimentally. The Runtime has a Windows build (64-bit Windows 10 or 11) that
is new and has not been through real use yet. In PowerShell, run
`irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Enlightened-Republic/Caelza/main/runtime/windows-install.ps1 | iex`
(`runtime/windows-install.ps1`). It checks the download, installs to

daemon` and open `http://127.0.0.1:42617` for Cael's setup (`Caelza-Setup.exe`
on the same release does all of this with a Start menu entry). Settings live in
`.caelza` in your user folder. If a release has no Windows build, the installer
says so. The Mind (long-term memory) has its own one-liner for Windows,
`mind/windows-install.ps1` (needs Node.js 22): it installs the brain service,

title: Caelza FAQ › Cael says he can't see Ollama. What is it, and what do I do?
content:
[Caelza FAQ › Cael says he can't see Ollama. What is it, and what do I do?]
Ollama is the free program that runs the local model on a computer (a phone
uses llama.cpp inside the app instead). On a PC the "free and local" door
needs it: Cael's setup page asks Ollama on the same computer what it has
(`http://127.0.0.1:11434`), and when nothing answers he shows a **Get Ollama**
link to `https://ollama.com/download`. Install it, leave it running (it sits in
the tray), and press **Check again**. Once it answers, the button becomes
**Download N GB and use this**: Cael pulls the model the ladder picked for your
memory (and his own 1.5B when it differs) with a progress bar, then sets the
agent up as "Use this" would. Only a page open on the computer itself can do
this; from another device Cael says so and gives the `ollama pull` line to run

title: The Mind › Caelza Mind — xanima
content:
[The Mind › Caelza Mind — xanima]
The Mind is Caelza's long-term memory. It is **xanima** (formerly openwave) on
the **xanima-core** engine (formerly sharpwave-core): a graph memory with an
FSRS forgetting curve, typed edges, supersession, beliefs with confidence and
provenance, a decision ledger, goals and drift checks, reflection, and a sleep
system (slow-wave / REM consolidation, awake replay, LLM fact extraction) that
improves the graph between sessions.

Airframe Lite already used the engine over MCP (`caelza_body/agent/memory.py`).
Caelza keeps the same engine and the same brain databases, so nothing migrates;
what changes is how the runtime reaches it.

title: The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body)
content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body)]
The Body is the device layer: termux-api sensors, ADB control of this phone
and paired phones, a shell, the web tools, and the self-modification tools,
all guarded by the immutable supervisor. Until now only the Python agent loop
could reach them. `caelza-body` serves the same tools over MCP so the
**Runtime** (`caelza`) can drive the phone directly (vision doc §3.1,
milestone M2).

```
caelza (Runtime)  ──stdio──▶  caelza-body serve  ──▶  termux-api / adb / sh / repo
                                  │
                                  └─ $CAELZA_BODY_HOME: devices.json, audit log,
                                     package snapshots, tmp captures
```

title: The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body)
content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body)]
Nothing about the tools changed. `caelza_body/agent/tools/*` register into one
registry; the agent loop reads it to build its function-calling schema, and
`caelza-body` reads the same registry to answer `tools/list`. The JSON schemas
pass through untouched, so a `reason` is still required where the Body
requires it, the audit log at `~/.caelza-body/logs/device-actions.log` still
gets every dangerous op, and `device_uninstall` / `device_disable` still
snapshot the package list and abort if the snapshot is empty.

title: The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Install and run
content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Install and run]
On the phone, in the Body checkout (`install.sh` already does the install):

```bash
pip install -e .            # puts `caelza-body` on PATH
caelza-body probe           # {"ok": true, "tools": 41, ...} and exit 0
caelza-body list-tools      # every tool, its schema and safety hints, as JSON
caelza-body serve           # the stdio server; this is what the Runtime runs
caelza-body serve --http    # the same over Streamable HTTP + a bearer token, for a hub (see Fleet)
caelza-body fleet           # the phones this Body reaches; `fleet join` adds a phone's Body
caelza-body playbooks       # the phone playbooks (body/sops); --install puts them where the Runtime loads SOPs
caelza-body runtime update  # the Runtime binary under the supervisor's guard: fetch a release, verify, probe, swap
```

title: The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Install and run
content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Install and run]
`--home DIR` overrides the state dir (default `$CAELZA_BODY_HOME`, then
`~/.caelza-body`), `--repo-root DIR` the checkout the `self_*` tools edit, and
`--tools selfmod,sensors,shell,device,web` picks the groups to expose. The
server reads the optional `[firecrawl]` / `[tavily]` / `[searchapi]` keys from
`config.toml` and needs nothing else from it: no Telegram token, no model.

Then merge [`caelza-body.example.toml`](caelza-body.example.toml) into
`~/.caelza/config.toml`: an `mcp.servers` entry named `body`, a bundle, the
grant to `agents.main`, and a risk profile. Tool names reach the agent as
`body__<tool>` (`body__device_list`).

content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Tools and their safety class]
The four `device_*` reads added for the playbooks (M5) live in
`caelza_body/agent/tools/playbook.py` and register with the `device` group:
`device_debloat_plan` (the curated debloat list applied to what is installed),
`device_suspects` (sideloaded apps with the permissions malware wants, scored),
`device_foreground` (what is on screen and who installed it) and
`device_health` (identity, battery, storage, memory, uptime, heat, crashes,
the setup checklist, in one adb call). Their parsing is pure code in

title: The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › How calls behave
content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › How calls behave]
- **Serialized.** One tool call runs at a time. The Body is one phone, and the
  tool functions block on `adb` / `termux-*` / `sh` for up to minutes, so they
  run on a worker thread while the server keeps answering pings.
- **Errors.** A tool that returns an `error: …` string (the Body's convention)
  comes back with `isError: true` and that text, so the Runtime treats it as a
  failed call rather than a result. Arguments are validated against the schema
  before the Body runs anything.
- **Images.** `device_screencap` and `sensors_camera_photo` return the picture
  as MCP image content plus a text block with the saved path under
  `~/.caelza-body/tmp/`. The Runtime carries image content as an attachment
  on the reply and never shows the base64 to the model. Captures older than

title: The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › How calls behave
content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › How calls behave]
  24 h are pruned on the next start.
- **Timeouts.** `tool_timeout_secs` in the Runtime config caps a call from the
  outside; the Body's own caps are `shell_run` 300 s, `sensors_mic_record`
  60 s, `device_screencap` 30 s.

title: The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Side by side with the agent loop
content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Side by side with the agent loop]
`caelza-body` does not replace the supervisor or the Python loop. On a phone
that runs Niba today, the supervisor keeps running the loop, and the Runtime
spawns `caelza-body` in addition. Both use the same tool code and the same
state dir, so pairing a device in one is visible in the other. Retiring the
loop (the rest of M2: the Runtime owns the turn, the supervisor guards the
Body code and the Runtime binary) is a per-phone switch once the Runtime is
running there (M1).

[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Fleet: a hub and its phones]
Deployment shape 2 (vision §3): the Runtime and the Mind on a hub, each phone
running only its Body. Two pieces, both in `caelza_body/fleet.py` (M6):

title: The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Fleet: a hub and its phones
content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Fleet: a hub and its phones]
**Serving.** `caelza-body serve --http` puts the same tools on Streamable
HTTP, the transport the Runtime's `transport = "http"` speaks, behind a
bearer token that is created on first run in `~/.caelza-body/run/http-token`
(mode 0600). It binds loopback unless `--host` says otherwise; the phone's
Tailscale address is the intended otherwise, and the server says so on
stderr. `/health` answers without the token (name, version, tool count) so
reachability and a bad token read differently; `/mcp` refuses anything but
the right `Authorization: Bearer`. Host headers are checked (DNS-rebinding
protection): the bind address and loopback by default, `--allow-host
niba.tail.ts.net` for a MagicDNS name.

**Reaching.** On the hub, `caelza-body fleet join grandma --url

title: The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Fleet: a hub and its phones
content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Fleet: a hub and its phones]
joined Body, and `body__device_uninstall` asks the owner either way. The
remote Body audit-logs and snapshots on its phone as if the agent ran there;
the hub adds one line per forwarded destructive call to `logs/fleet.log`,
with a `token` or `code` argument redacted. Only a tool whose schema has a
`device` argument is forwarded: `device_join(..., device="grandma")` names no
phone to run on, so it stays local and is refused there, and a joined phone's
token never travels in a stray argument. The registry file is re-read when
another process wrote it, so `caelza-body fleet join` beside a running Body
is seen at once and kept by the Body's next save; a name cannot flip between
a paired phone and a joined Body without `device_unpair` first; token files
are created 0600 inside 0700 directories.

content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Fleet: a hub and its phones]

and `tests/test_android_body.py`). The fleet tools stay here: the app's Body

title: The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Fleet: a hub and its phones
content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Fleet: a hub and its phones]
`device_list` shows the fleet with kinds (`self`, `adb`, `http`), reachability
(a remote's `/health`) and **groups**. `device_pair … groups="family"`,
`device_tag`, or `caelza-body fleet tag grandma --groups family` set them; the
Procedures page's Run offers "every phone in family" and starts one run per

title: The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Fleet: a hub and its phones
content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Fleet: a hub and its phones]
[`../runtime/caelza.hub.example.toml`](../runtime/caelza.hub.example.toml) is
the hub's Runtime config: the hub's own `caelza-body serve` is the Body the
Runtime talks to, with the joined phones behind it. A phone can also be a

`headers.Authorization`); its tools then arrive as `body-grandma__<tool>`,
which the Bodies page lists but the playbooks do not name, so the fleet Body
is the recommended path. Keep the HTTP endpoint behind Tailscale or a
firewall: the token is the only lock.

title: The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › The Runtime under the guard
content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › The Runtime under the guard]
Vision §3.5: the Runtime binary is built by CI from this repo
(`.github/workflows/release.yml`), and the supervisor pulls it onto the phone
the way the Body's own code is promoted. `caelza_body/runtime_guard.py`,
stdlib only and as immutable as the supervisor, does the work (M6):

```sh
caelza-body runtime update            # the latest release for this machine (GITHUB_TOKEN for a private repo)
caelza-body runtime update --tag v0.1.0
caelza-body runtime update --archive caelza-0.1.0-aarch64-linux-android.tar.gz   # no network
caelza-body runtime status            # current, last-good, what is installed
caelza-body runtime rollback          # current -> last-good, by hand
caelza-body runtime link              # $PREFIX/bin/caelza -> the current binary
```

title: The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › The Runtime under the guard
content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › The Runtime under the guard]
`update` finds the release's archive for this target (`aarch64-linux-android`
in Termux), downloads it and its `.sha256`, verifies, unpacks into
`~/.caelza-body/runtime/<version>/` (refusing an archive that escapes its
directory), and **probes** the new binary before trusting it: `caelza
--version` must answer with the release's version, and `caelza gateway start`
on a probe port must serve `/health` within a minute. Only then it snapshots
`~/.caelza` (the config, the agents' files, the shared SOPs and skills; never
the data) into `~/.caelza-body/snapshots/`, points `current` and `last-good`
at the version, and asks the supervisor to restart the Runtime. A binary that
does not hold is deleted and the one running stays current; nothing else is
touched.

title: The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › The Runtime under the guard
content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › The Runtime under the guard]
The probe runs the new gateway on a **copy** of `~/.caelza` (the config, its
`.secret_key`, the shared SOPs and skills, the agents' files minus their
workspaces) in the work dir: the live dir belongs to the Runtime that is
running, which holds its lock and its data there. The probe also refuses a
probe port that something else already answers on, so a stale gateway can
never vouch for a new binary. `update` moves `current` to the new version and
leaves `last-good` on the version that was running; the supervisor promotes
the new one to `last-good` once it has held for ten minutes. A version that
is current is never reinstalled over itself, and `prune` keeps current,
last-good and the version still running.

The supervisor runs `caelza daemon` from `runtime/current` as a child beside

title: The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › The Runtime under the guard
content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › The Runtime under the guard]
the agent, restarts it when the guard asks, and on a crash loop points
`current` back at `last-good` and restarts it; a crash loop on last-good
itself halts the Runtime and alerts for a human, the same ladder the Body's
own code gets. A later `runtime update` (or `runtime rollback`) revives a
halted Runtime: its restart request is read first. Before blaming a crash
loop on the binary the supervisor checks whether another Runtime already
answers on the gateway port (a `caelza daemon` started by hand, or by an old
Termux:Boot script): then it halts without rolling back and says so. Whatever
goes wrong inside the Runtime guard is alerted, never raised, so the agent's
own ladder keeps running; Ctrl-C, SIGTERM and an unexpected error all end

content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › The Runtime under the guard]
with the children stopped. With no runtime installed the supervisor leaves
the Runtime to whatever runs it today (the Termux:Boot script from

connection to it for the gateway's lifetime and makes the tool calls with the

title: The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › The phone playbooks (sops/)
content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › The phone playbooks (sops/)]
Four standard operating procedures for the Runtime's SOP engine, the Airframe
capability playbooks as procedures with approval gates (milestone M5):
`phone-debloat`, `phone-malware-removal`, `phone-new-setup`,
`phone-diagnostics`. Each is a `SOP.toml` + `SOP.md` directory the Runtime
loads as-is; the reads are the playbook tools above, the one step per
procedure that changes the phone carries `requires_confirmation` and parks the
run until the owner approves it on the Procedures page (which gives each a
**Run** that asks which phone), on Home, or over `caelza sop approve`.
`caelza-body playbooks --install` copies them into `~/.caelza/shared/sops`,
`install.sh` does the same on a phone, and `[sop] sops_dir = "shared/sops"`
in the Runtime config loads them. [`sops/README.md`](sops/README.md) has the

title: The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › The phone playbooks (sops/)
content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › The phone playbooks (sops/)]
table, the gates, the evals and how to run them against an emulator.

The reads behind them err on the owner's side: `device_debloat_plan` reads
who installed each third-party package and sends one the owner installed from
a store to `review` even when the table knows its name as a carrier preload;
`device_suspects` and `device_foreground` read ordinary device admins (the
`pkg/.Receiver:` lines, not only owners), grep the sensitive permissions
before the list is cut, and do not call a preload a sideload; every remote
script must come back with its end marker, or it is reported as cut off
rather than parsed short.

title: The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Forge
content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Forge]
The agent improves its own engine without holding the compiler (vision §3.5,
M6; [`../docs/forge.md`](../docs/forge.md) is the walkthrough). Two
procedures in `sops/` and a tool group close the loop:

- `forge-propose` frames a Runtime change, reads the files as they are on
  `main`, drafts the new content and the pull request, and after the owner's
  gate writes a `forge/<topic>` branch and a **draft PR** through
  `git_forge`, the Runtime's forge tool over its git channel (a GitHub App on
  the repo; [`../runtime/caelza.forge.example.toml`](../runtime/caelza.forge.example.toml)).
  CI builds and tests the branch; a human merges; a `v*` tag releases.
- `forge-release` starts from the channel's `release.published` event (or by
  hand with a tag): it reads the release and whether this machine's archive

title: The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Forge
content:
[The Body › Caelza Body as an MCP server (caelza-body) › Forge]
  is in it, tells the owner, and after their gate calls `runtime_update`.
- The `runtime` group (`caelza-body serve --tools …,runtime`, on the machine
  that runs the Runtime): `runtime_status` is `caelza-body runtime status`
  plus whether an update is running and the tail of its log;
  `runtime_update(reason, tag?)` starts `caelza-body runtime update` detached
  (the guard above does the rest and the supervisor restarts the Runtime),
  logging to `logs/runtime-update.log` and auditing the reason. It is
  destructive and always asks.

The release workflow builds every archive with `--features channel-git`
(upstream keeps the git channel out of its lean default), and `build.sh`
passes the same flag.

title: Runtime docs › Caelza
content:
[Runtime docs › Caelza]
Personal AI assistant you own, written in Rust.

Caelza is an agent runtime: a single binary you configure and run. It talks to LLM providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Ollama, and ~20 others), reaches the world through channels (Discord, Telegram, Matrix, email, voice, webhooks, your own CLI), and acts through tools (shell, browser, HTTP, hardware, custom MCP servers). Everything runs on your machine, with your keys, in your workspace.

Read [Philosophy](./philosophy/index.md) to understand the opinions that shape it.

This site is the documentation. Everything under **Reference → CLI** and **Reference → Config** is generated directly from the code at build time (via `clap` derives and the JSON schema), so it stays in sync with the binary you actually run. Everything else is hand-written user-facing material.

Where to start:

title: Runtime docs › Concepts
content:
[Runtime docs › Concepts]
These are the terms Quickstart and the config reference assume. Each one has a deeper page linked at the end of its definition.

**Alias.** An alias is the name you assign to a configured instance, then
reference elsewhere to point at it. You choose the name freely; other parts of
the config wire things together by that name. Aliases are lowercase ASCII
letters, digits, and single underscores, must start and end with a letter or
digit, and cannot contain `__` or hyphens. In the config they appear as the
`<alias>` segment of a section header, such as `[agents.<alias>]` or
`[providers.models.<type>.<alias>]`. See
[Reference → Environment variables → Alias grammar](../reference/env-vars.md#alias-grammar).

title: Runtime docs › Concepts
content:
[Runtime docs › Concepts]
**Model provider.** A model provider is Caelza's abstraction over an LLM
endpoint. Every chat-completion request goes through a provider, whether the
target is a remote API, a self-hosted server, or a local Ollama model.
Providers are typed by vendor family, and you can run several named instances
of the same family. In the config each one lives at
`[providers.models.<type>.<alias>]`. See
[Model Providers → Overview](../providers/overview.md).

**Risk profile.** A risk profile is a named autonomy and sandbox posture. Its
level is `readonly`, `supervised` (the default), or `full`, controlling whether
tools run automatically, prompt for approval, or are blocked. Each agent
references exactly one risk profile. In the config it lives at
`[risk_profiles.<alias>]`. See
[Security → Autonomy Levels](../security/autonomy.md).

title: Runtime docs › Concepts
content:
[Runtime docs › Concepts]
**Runtime profile.** A runtime profile is reusable operational tuning: agentic
mode, tool-iteration caps, action and cost budgets, timeouts, context limits,
and delegation policy. It is separate from the risk profile, which governs
autonomy. Quickstart installs the `unbounded` preset for new agents; adjust the
fields afterward. In the config it lives at `[runtime_profiles.<alias>]`. See
[Reference → Config](../reference/config.md).

title: Runtime docs › Concepts
content:
[Runtime docs › Concepts]
**Multi-agent.** Caelza runs many agents from one install. Each agent has its
own set of references (risk profile, model provider, channels), its own
workspace directory, and its own memory backend. An agent can spawn an
ephemeral **SubAgent** that inherits its parent's identity and security policy,
and agents can talk to each other when they share a **peer group**. In the
config each agent is an `[agents.<alias>]` block. See
[Agents → Runtime internals](../agents/internals.md).

**Peer group.** A peer group declares an opt-in cross-agent communication set on
a single channel. Membership is mutual: two agents are peers only when both
appear in the same group's member list. In the config it lives at
`[peer_groups.<name>]`. See
[Agents → Runtime internals](../agents/internals.md).

title: Runtime docs › Concepts
content:
[Runtime docs › Concepts]
**Skill bundle.** A skill bundle is a reusable group of skills attached to an
agent or channel by alias. It controls which skills load and from where: a
source directory plus optional include and exclude lists. Skills themselves are
reusable instructions and optional tool definitions. In the config a bundle
lives at `[skill_bundles.<alias>]`. See [Tools → Skills](../tools/skills.md).

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart]
Quickstart is the guided setup that takes you from a fresh install to a working
agent in one pass. It runs on three surfaces: the **CLI**, the **caelcode**
terminal interface, and the **web gateway**. All three drive the same
underlying flow, so the config they produce is identical. Use whichever fits
where you are.

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › Install › Unix fast path
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › Install › Unix fast path]
```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Enlightened-Republic/caelza/master/install.sh | sh
```

This route is noninteractive and does not open a picker.

It prefers a matching prebuilt binary and falls back to a source build when needed.

A prebuilt archive may contain caelcode; a noninteractive source fallback installs the default app without opening a picker.

The command uses a fixed feature set.

If a source build is needed, the installer can bootstrap Rust when it is missing.

On Unix, the installer updates the shell profile when allowed; reload the parent shell before relying on the new PATH.

The installer skips setup and prints `caelza quickstart` as the next step.

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › Install › Unix guided path
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › Install › Unix guided path]
```sh
git clone https://github.com/Enlightened-Republic/caelza.git
cd caelza
./install.sh
```

This route is guided and may offer supported choices.

On supported targets, it offers prebuilt or source installation.

A prebuilt archive may contain caelcode; a source choice selects it by default and allows app selection.

The source path also lets you select optional Cargo features.

If a source build is needed, the installer can bootstrap Rust when it is missing.

On Unix, the installer updates the shell profile when allowed; reload the parent shell before relying on the new PATH.

For an unconfigured install, it offers `caelza quickstart` or browser-based Quickstart.

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › Install › Windows prebuilt path
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › Install › Windows prebuilt path]
Use the PowerShell block in the [Windows setup guide](../setup/windows.md). Installation and PATH setup are idempotent; Quickstart still runs.

This route is noninteractive and does not open a picker.

This route installs a prebuilt release archive.

The archive may also contain caelcode; availability depends on the release asset.

The command uses a fixed feature set.

This prebuilt route does not require a Rust toolchain.

On Windows, the PowerShell path updates the current process and the persistent user PATH.

The PowerShell block finishes by running `caelza quickstart` automatically.

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › Install › Advanced source path › Unix
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › Install › Advanced source path › Unix]
```sh
./install.sh --source
```

This route is guided and may offer supported choices.

This route always builds from source.

Source installation selects caelcode by default and lets you change the app selection.

The source path also lets you select optional Cargo features.

If a source build is needed, the installer can bootstrap Rust when it is missing.

On Unix, the installer updates the shell profile when allowed; reload the parent shell before relying on the new PATH.

For an unconfigured install, it offers `caelza quickstart` or browser-based Quickstart.

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › Install › Advanced source path › Windows
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › Install › Advanced source path › Windows]
```powershell
cargo install --locked --path .
```

This route is noninteractive and does not open a picker.

This route always builds from source.

This command installs the core `caelza` binary; it does not install optional apps.

The command uses a fixed feature set.

A Rust toolchain is required before using this command.

This Cargo command does not edit PATH; make sure Cargo's bin directory is already available in your shell.

After installation, run `caelza quickstart`.

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › The steps
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › The steps]
> **Important:** if any of these terms are unfamiliar, read
> [Getting Started → Concepts](./concepts.md) first. It defines model
> provider, risk profile, alias, and the rest in one place.

Every surface walks the same checklist and writes the same config; only the
optional Plugins step is CLI-only for now. Required steps must be satisfied
before the agent can be created; optional steps can be skipped.

| Step | Required | What it sets |
|---|---|---|
| **Model provider** | yes | Provider family (Anthropic, OpenAI, Ollama, OpenRouter, …), its API key or endpoint, and the model. |
| **Risk profile** | yes | Autonomy and sandbox posture. Pick a preset or reuse an existing `[risk_profiles.<alias>]`. |
| **Memory** | yes | Memory backend (`sqlite`, `markdown`, `postgres`, `qdrant`, `lucid`, or `none`). |

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › The steps
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › The steps]
| **Channels** | optional | Chat platforms (Telegram, Discord, Slack, …). The built-in `cli` channel always works; add others here or later. |
| **Peer groups** | optional | Multi-agent peer membership for the channels you configured. |
| **Plugins** | optional | Tool plugins from the plugin registry, installed and configured when the agent is created. Only in builds with WASM plugin support (`plugins-wasm`), and only in the CLI Quickstart for now; see [Plugins](../getting-started/quickstart.md#plugins). |
| **Agent** | yes | Agent alias, system prompt, and any personality files. |

> The runtime profile is set automatically. Quickstart installs the
> `unbounded` preset for the new agent. Tune budgets and timeouts afterward by
> editing `[runtime_profiles.<alias>]` (see
> [Reference → Config](../reference/config.md)).

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI]
The fastest path on a headless box or over SSH:

**sh**
```sh
caelza quickstart
```

You answer one prompt per step in the terminal. The built-in `cli` channel
works immediately, so Channels and Peer groups can be skipped. For an
all-defaults, no-approvals config, see [YOLO mode](./yolo.md).

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › OpenAI Codex subscription auth
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › OpenAI Codex subscription auth]
Quickstart can configure the OpenAI Codex subscription path without an API key.
Authenticate once, then choose **OpenAI** as the provider and set
**Authentication** to `codex` when prompted:

```sh
# If you already signed in with the Codex CLI:
caelza auth login --model-provider openai-codex --import ~/.codex/auth.json

# Or start Caelza's own OpenAI Codex login flow:
caelza auth login --model-provider openai-codex
```

For scripted setup, `openai-codex` is accepted as a quickstart input alias and
writes the canonical `[providers.models.openai.<alias>]` entry:

```sh
caelza quickstart --model-provider openai-codex --model gpt-5.4 --agent assistant
```

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Claude subscription setup-token auth
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Claude subscription setup-token auth]
Quickstart can also configure Claude/Anthropic with a normal Console API key
or a token generated by Claude Max:

```sh
claude setup-token
caelza quickstart --model-provider anthropic --model claude-sonnet-4-5 --agent assistant
```

Choose **Anthropic**, set **Authentication** to `setup_token`, then paste the
token from `claude setup-token` into the API key/token prompt. Scripted input
may use `--model-provider claude` as an alias. Quickstart still writes the
canonical `[providers.models.anthropic.<alias>]` entry; the token is stored
through the same credential path as `api_key`.

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
Builds with WASM plugin support add an optional **Plugins** row to the CLI
checklist, after **Peer groups**. The row exists only when the binary is built
with the `plugins-wasm` feature. Today's release archives are built without it,
so their checklist has no Plugins row; a source build with `--preset full` and
the `all-features` container image include it. Only the CLI Quickstart offers
the row for now: the caelcode and web gateway Quickstart do not list plugins
yet. Leaving the row unvisited changes nothing.

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
Opening the row fetches the plugin registry index, the same one
`caelza plugin search` uses (set `CAELZA_PLUGIN_REGISTRY_URL` to use another
registry), and lists every tool plugin the registry offers or this machine
already has, marking the installed ones. If the registry index cannot be
fetched, you can retry or continue without plugins. Picking plugins downloads
no package and changes no config. Opening the row only writes the registry
index cache under the data directory, as `caelza plugin search` does, and
creates the plugins directory if it is missing.

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
If Quickstart could not read the `[plugins]` section of the config file,
because that section or the whole file is malformed, the row says so instead
of fetching the registry. It offers nothing to pick, and **Create** installs no
plugin. Repair the file, then run Quickstart again to install plugins.

If the config file was written by an older Caelza version, **Create** stops
before installing any plugin or creating the agent, and prints the
`caelza config migrate` command that updates the file, as `caelza plugin
bind` does. Run that command, then run Quickstart again. Saving plugin settings
into the older file would mark it as current without moving its older
settings, which later runs would then stop reading.

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
When you choose **Create**, Quickstart installs the picked plugins before it
creates the agent. First it checks the rest of your choices, and the
configuration they land in, the way the agent step will, including the
authorization check the agent step runs before it writes anything. If the
agent step would refuse them, for example because a permission profile names
an agent that no longer exists, Quickstart reports the problems and stops
before any plugin is downloaded or written. Then it installs the plugins one
at a time, through the pipeline `caelza plugin install` uses:

1. It resolves the package from the registry and refuses a registry entry that
   has no `sha256` digest for its archive, before requesting the archive.
   `caelza plugin install` checks the digest only when the registry lists
   one; Quickstart requires it.

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
2. It downloads and verifies the archive, confirms that the manifest provides a
   tool, admits the package, checks that its config entry can be seeded, and
   runs the install-time load check. When any of these steps fails, Quickstart
   reports it, writes nothing for that plugin, and moves on to the next one.
   The config entry check fails, for example, when the config still holds the
   plugin's pre-1.0 entry, named only after the package, which
   `caelza plugin remove` keeps: `caelza plugin install` refuses to create
   an entry beside it, and Quickstart reports the same reason before it asks
   anything about the plugin. Quickstart has no `--no-verify`: for a plugin
   that fails the load check it prints the
   `caelza plugin install <name> --no-verify` command, which installs a

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
   plugin that the daemon then skips at startup. That command is the plugin
   CLI, not Quickstart: it asks no signature question and no network access
   question, and a config entry it creates is seeded with the destinations the
   manifest declares for `http_client`.
3. It prints what the plugin is and what it asks for: name, version, author,
   description, capabilities, permissions, and the network destinations its
   manifest declares. Publisher text is stripped of terminal control sequences
   first.
4. It checks the manifest signature against
   `plugins.security.trusted_publisher_keys`, whatever
   `plugins.security.signature_mode` is, and adds one line to that summary:
   verified, with the first 16 characters of the trusted key; unsigned; signed
   under a key that is not trusted; or invalid. Unless the signature is

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
   verified, the author line is marked as the publisher's own claim, and
   Quickstart asks whether to install the plugin anyway before any other
   question about it. The answer defaults to no, which skips the plugin and
   writes nothing. `signature_mode` still decides what admission refuses: in
   `strict` mode such a plugin is refused at step 2 instead. When Quickstart
   can read the plugins directory, a picked plugin that is already installed
   shows the same line, without the question.
5. For a plugin that requests `http_client` and declares destinations, you
   choose to grant the declared destinations, install without network access,
   or skip the plugin. The choice starts on installing without network access,
   so accepting it as offered grants nothing. Installing without network

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
   access creates the plugin's config entry with an empty `egress_hosts`, so
   the plugin reaches nothing, and prints the exact `caelza config set`
   command that grants the declared destinations later. It is the decision
   `caelza plugin bind --egress none` records for a channel instance, and
   it prints the same command. A plugin that requests network access but
   declares no destinations gets no question; after installing it, Quickstart
   prints a `caelza config set --no-interactive` command for the entry's
   `egress_hosts` with no value: append the hosts your deployment uses as one
   comma-separated value. Run as printed, that command is refused for the
   missing value and writes nothing. A plugin that declares destinations and
   requests `websocket_client` or `socket_client` but not `http_client` gets

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
   no question either: its config entry grants none of them, and Quickstart
   prints the `caelza config set` command that grants exactly those
   destinations.
6. For a plugin whose manifest has a `config_schema`, Quickstart prompts for
   the settings it describes: required properties first, optional ones only if
   you ask for them. Properties marked `x-secret` are masked as you type them,
   and spaces or line breaks around a secret value are dropped, as
   `caelza config set` drops them. A value picked from a list is stored
   exactly as the schema lists it, an empty string included, while an empty
   typed answer leaves an optional setting unset. The values are checked
   against the schema
   before anything is written; after a failed check you get one more try, then

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
   Quickstart asks whether to install the plugin without them. Pressing Esc at
   a required setting that is secret or picked from a list skips the plugin.
   Quickstart prompts only for properties whose names are in the portable key
   grammar (up to 128 ASCII letters, digits, `.`, `-` and `_`). It names the
   others so that you can set them later with `caelza config set`. When a
   required property is one of them, or a name the schema requires without
   declaring it, no answers could pass the check, so Quickstart asks for no
   settings and goes straight to asking whether to install the plugin without
   them. When the schema requires a name it does not declare, no config entry
   can satisfy it, whatever `caelza config set` writes, so that question
   says the plugin's tool would not be usable and asks whether to install it
   anyway.

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
7. It publishes the package and seeds its config entry in the same transaction
   `caelza plugin install` uses, then saves the settings the way
   `caelza config set` does. If seeding the entry fails, the transaction
   removes the package again. If that removal fails too, Quickstart says the
   plugin is still installed and prints the `caelza plugin remove` command
   for it. If saving the settings fails, the plugin stays installed, and
   Quickstart prints the `caelza config set` command for each setting,
   which asks for the value. A plugin that also provides a channel gets what
   `caelza plugin install` prints for it: the `caelza plugin bind`
   commands that bind an instance, or the readiness of the aliases that
   already bind the package. Quickstart binds no channel instance itself.

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
Values you type for settings that are not marked `x-secret` are echoed at the
prompt, and a default from the schema is prefilled there. Setting values are
never written to logs or to the status lines Quickstart prints; those name the
settings only.

A plugin that is already installed is not downloaded, upgraded, or prompted for
settings again. Quickstart only creates its config entry when that entry is
missing. A new entry is a new grant, so for a plugin that requests
`http_client` and declares destinations you first see what the plugin is and
make the same choice as for a fresh install: grant the declared destinations,
create the entry without network access, or skip, which leaves the entry absent
and prints the command that creates it later. That command creates the entry

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
without network access. The command that grants the declared destinations is
printed on its own line, to run after it, so running a printed command never
grants what you declined. Any other missing entry is seeded as
`caelza plugin install` seeds it. An existing entry is never changed,
whether it belongs to an installed plugin or was left behind by an earlier
install, so its egress grant and settings stay exactly as they are. Running
Quickstart again with the same picks therefore downloads nothing and leaves
those entries untouched. If Quickstart cannot finish setting up a plugin that
is already installed, for example because the config still holds a pre-1.0
entry named only after the package or because saving the new entry fails, it
writes nothing for that plugin and says that the plugin stays installed, with
the reason.

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
After the last plugin, if at least one picked plugin is installed and
`plugins.enabled` or `plugins.auto_discover` is off, Quickstart asks once
whether to turn plugin activation on. First it lists which of those settings
would change and everything that would become active as a result: every
installed tool and skill plugin, including plugins installed before this run,
and, when `plugins.enabled` is off, every enabled `[channels.plugin.<alias>]`
channel. The list is read from the plugins directory, as a daemon would load
it at its next start, so it also names a plugin whose failed install could not
be undone. Each listed plugin whose signature is not verified is followed by
its signature line from step 4, including a plugin this run did not pick.
The answer defaults to yes when the list matches the plugins this run

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
installed or kept, and to no when it would activate anything else, including an
installed plugin whose missing config entry you chose to skip or that
Quickstart could not finish setting up. If the plugins
directory cannot be read, Quickstart says the list may be incomplete and the
answer defaults to no. Declining leaves
both settings unchanged and prints the `caelza config set` commands that turn
them on later. When both settings are already on, there is nothing to ask.

Once the agent is created, Quickstart prints the status of each picked plugin
that is installed: admitted as a tool, with its config entry key, or the
reason it is not admitted, such as `plugins.enabled` or
`plugins.auto_discover` being off or the `plugins.max_active_instances` limit
being reached. A plugin is reported admitted only when its config entry passes

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
the settings check the runtime applies on every call. Admitted is not yet
registered: the tool registry registers the plugin when it is next built, and
it still refuses a package whose name clashes with a tool already registered,
such as a built-in tool, or whose tool description it cannot read. The runtime
log records those refusals. When the settings check fails instead, for example
when you installed the plugin without its required settings, its status shows
the reason the check gives,
names the required settings that are missing, and prints the
`caelza config set` command that asks for each value. Quickstart prints
commands only for setting names in the portable key grammar, which are safe to
show and to paste into a shell. A required setting with any other name is
named without a command: set it in the config file, or with a

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
`caelza config set` command you quote yourself. A required name that the
plugin's schema does not declare is named too, since no config entry can
satisfy that schema until the plugin's publisher fixes it. A plugin whose
config entry is missing, for example because you skipped creating it, is not
reported active either: `caelza config set` only changes entries that exist,
so its status prints the command that creates the entry instead. That command
grants no network access; for a plugin that requests `http_client` and
declares destinations, a separate line gives the command that grants them once
the entry exists. When the config still holds the plugin's pre-1.0 entry,
named only after the package, its status prints neither command, since a new
entry beside the old one would leave the old entry's settings and network grant

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
behind. It names the instance key to rename the old entry to instead. When
`caelza plugin list` prints the update steps for that entry, which it does
for a plugin that requests `http_client` unless the deployment refuses every
plugin's network grant, the status also gives that command: its steps include
any network grant the renamed entry still needs. A plugin with nothing to
configure and no network access needs no config entry.

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
A picked plugin that was already installed may never have passed the load
check, for example when it was installed with
`caelza plugin install --no-verify`, so Quickstart runs the check
`caelza plugin info` runs before it reports the plugin. When the plugin does
not load against this host, Caelza skips it at startup, so its status says
that instead of calling it active and gives the `caelza plugin info` command
that shows why.

Quickstart writes the config file and never signals a running daemon. A daemon
that is already running keeps the configuration it loaded, so the config
entries, settings, network grants, and plugin activation changes a Quickstart
run writes reach it only after it restarts or reloads its configuration. If
plugin activation was already on in the configuration the daemon loaded, it can

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
load a newly installed plugin sooner, the next time it builds its tool registry
(for example for a new session). It then runs the plugin with the config entry
it had loaded for that plugin, never one the run wrote: without one, the plugin
has no settings and no network grant, and an older entry, such as one that
`caelza plugin remove` kept from an earlier install, applies with its
settings and network grant. The status ends with the `caelza service restart`
command, addressed to the same configuration directory, which restarts a daemon
that runs as the installed service.
`caelza agent` and other one-shot commands pick the changes up the next time
they start.

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
Ctrl+C does not work the same everywhere in the plugin step. At a secret setting
it works like Esc: at a required setting it cancels that plugin's settings, so
the plugin is skipped, and at an optional one it leaves the setting unset.
Quickstart then carries on. Anywhere else in the step, Ctrl+C ends Quickstart
at once, without a summary of what it already did. A plugin whose install
finished stays installed and configured, and `caelza plugin list` shows it.
A plugin interrupted after its install but before its config entry was written
stays installed without that entry; running Quickstart again with the same pick
creates the entry, asking first when it would grant network destinations.

title: Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins
content:
[Runtime docs › Quickstart › CLI › Plugins]
If the agent step still fails after the plugin step changed something,
Quickstart does not claim that nothing changed. It names the plugins that stay
installed, configured, or activated, and prints the `caelza plugin remove`
command for each plugin that run installed, including one whose failed install
could not be undone and so stays in the plugins directory. Running Quickstart
again does not reinstall them.
